new_entities.name: Glycogen supercompensation
new_entities.description: A pre-endurance-event strategy that raises muscle glycogen stores through several days of high carbohydrate intake, sometimes after a depletion session.

new_entities.name: Marathon finish time
new_entities.description: How long it takes a runner to complete a marathon-distance race.

edges.effect_quant: Direct marathon-finish-time trials are sparse, but modern endurance reviews still treat carbohydrate loading as the standard way to raise glycogen availability before marathon-length events. Older experiments suggest glycogen supercompensation supports longer endurance performance, whereas a much shorter 10 km time trial did not improve after only modest carbohydrate manipulation.
edges.population: trained endurance runners and other athletes competing in events long enough for glycogen depletion to become performance-limiting
edges.mechanism: Carbohydrate loading increases starting muscle glycogen, which delays the point at which pace must be reduced because carbohydrate availability becomes limiting. That logic matters much more in marathon-length competition than in shorter events where glycogen depletion is less decisive.
edges.summary: This is a classic endurance-sports edge where the physiology is stronger than the direct marathon RCT literature. The boring conclusion is still that glycogen supercompensation is worth doing for marathon-length races, but the strongest direct experiments are older and often use endurance surrogates rather than modern marathon finish-time designs.
edges.caveats: Evidence is more convincing for prolonged events than for shorter races. A null 10 km running trial should not be overgeneralized to the marathon, but it does argue against assuming that any high-carbohydrate week automatically improves performance regardless of event duration and protocol quality.
